claims.text: In refractory HEAs, lattice distortion is the dominant factor controlling high-temperature mechanical and thermoelastic behavior, rather than changes in dislocation core configuration.
NbTaTiV can form a single-phase BCC refractory HEA.
The baseline NbTaTiV alloy is equiatomic or near-equiatomic.
The baseline NbTaTiV alloy has moderate lattice distortion.
Substituting a refractory element with one having a significantly larger atomic radius will increase lattice distortion.
Electronic character and phase stability can be kept sufficiently similar during the proposed substitution to isolate lattice distortion.
Increased atomic-size mismatch induces enhanced heterogeneous lattice strain fields.
Greater lattice distortion increases local strain heterogeneity.
Local strain heterogeneity stiffens the elastic response.
Greater lattice distortion alters thermoelastic moduli and elastic anisotropy under high-temperature loading.
Heterogeneous strain fields interact with dislocations and thereby strengthen compositionally complex alloys.
The higher-distortion modified alloy will have higher yield strength than the baseline alloy.
The higher-distortion modified alloy will exhibit a distinct shift in thermoelastic moduli and lattice-strain evolution relative to the baseline.
The modified and baseline alloys will retain similar dislocation core structures.
In-situ neutron diffraction can determine elastic moduli, elastic anisotropy, and lattice-strain evolution in BCC NbTaTiV at elevated temperatures.

The proposed causal comparison applies specifically from 673 to 873 K when both alloys remain single-phase BCC, precipitation and phase instabilities are absent, and dislocation core features are unaltered.
